Imagine you bought an ETF tracking Japanese equities last week when the Nikkei 225 was already sliding; your order filled at the ask, but the quoted spread had just widened from 4 cents to 18 cents in the first 20 minutes of trading. The mechanism at work is liquidity withdrawal by market makers when overnight news (in this case rate worries and regional equity weakness) increases perceived risk, so the displayed bid drops faster than the ask can be hit. What most retail investors don’t realize is that the effective spread you actually pay can be two to three times the displayed quote once you factor in the depth at each level—checking Level 2 data before market open reveals whether the inside market is one-sided. The professionals always compare the current spread to the 20-day average before entering; if it is more than 50% wider, they either wait or use a limit order at the midpoint. The biggest mistake with spread dynamics is assuming the posted quote is the cost you will pay. Instead, always pull up the time-and-sales tape for the prior 15 minutes and size your order to no more than 20% of the visible depth at the bid.

S&P 500 closed at seven thousand four hundred thirty one up zero point five percent. NASDAQ closed at twenty five thousand eight hundred eighty nine up zero point three percent. TSX Composite closed at thirty four thousand nine hundred thirty eight up zero point eight percent.

Index levels were unavailable from the live feed on a couple of days but the pattern held with broad gains on geopolitical relief and rotation into financials and consumer discretionary.

The single most consequential thread was the return of risk appetite after the Hormuz deal and how that reshaped both oil and equity spreads.

That relief set the stage for the twenty two billion dollar Fox Roku transaction to stand out as a clean M&A arbitrage opportunity.

Roku shares traded at a discount to the cash and stock offer creating a defined outcome position that profits if the deal closes on schedule.

The strategy calls for sizing the position to two to three percent of the portfolio and pairing it with an index short or put spread to neutralize broad market moves.

Historical returns in low volatility periods have run between five and twelve percent annualized when regulatory risk stays minimal.

Canadian investors can replicate the same approach inside a TFSA once the deal terms appear in the brokerage corporate actions feed.

This is the exact scenario where our earlier rule about volume confirmation would have helped because acquisition catalysts need that confirmation to withstand sector rotations.

The same risk on environment also favored income strategies over pure directional bets as futures stayed subdued.

A covered call ETF approach lets investors sell thirty delta monthly calls on QQQ or XIU to collect eight to twelve percent annualized yield on top of any capital appreciation.

Implementation starts on platforms like Questrade or Interactive Brokers by selecting the broad equity ETF and selling the calls at the thirty delta strike each month.

The premium arrives regardless of modest upside but the main risk is opportunity cost if the underlying rallies sharply above the strike.

Size the covered calls so they represent no more than twenty to thirty percent of total equity exposure to preserve upside participation.

This approach has historically performed best in range bound or mildly bullish markets where the underlying drifts sideways.

Tokenization of NYSE and NASDAQ shares also gained traction as a way to access twenty four seven settlement once regulators clear the structures.

The approach can reduce overnight gaps during volatile periods but carries custody and regulatory risks until clearer North American rules emerge.

Start by paper trading the concept on any available fractional share platform to understand settlement mechanics before committing capital.

Core satellite construction gained fresh attention as a way to anchor seventy to eighty percent in XEQT or VTI slash VXUS while allocating twenty to thirty percent to targeted sleeves.

Rebalance the satellite sleeve quarterly or when any position doubles in weight and sell once the catalyst has been fully priced in.

This tactic has historically worked best in low volatility periods when management has high conviction in free cash flow stability.

Canada's Nuvei announced a two point seven five billion dollar acquisition of Payoneer to expand its cross border payments reach. The transaction targets Payoneer's existing merchant base and adds scale in emerging markets where Nuvei has limited presence. Deal documents filed with regulators show the purchase will be funded through a mix of cash and new equity issuance.

Payoneer shares traded at a modest premium to the offer price immediately after announcement reflecting market expectations for quick regulatory clearance. Investors tracking similar cross border fintech deals can monitor SEDAR+ for the formal arrangement agreement expected within thirty days.

The stock reaction highlights how even large strategic purchases can pressure multiples when accompanied by any earnings caution. Investors following professional services names can watch for similar forecast adjustments in upcoming quarterly updates from peers.

The deal itself remains accretive on a multi year basis according to the company's internal projections.

The purchase brings Blue Canyon's existing NASA and defense contracts into MDA's orbit and creates cross selling opportunities for Canadian geospatial data services. Terms include an upfront cash component plus earn out provisions tied to future revenue milestones.

Blue Canyon shareholders approved the transaction earlier this month clearing one regulatory hurdle. Canadian investors can access the combined entity through MDA's TSX listing once the deal closes later this summer. The move strengthens MDA's position in the growing small satellite supply chain.

Investors with exposure to Canadian exporters can review company filings for contingency language around tariff scenarios. The outcome will also influence Bank of Canada growth forecasts released later this summer.

Professionals always check the 20-day average dollar volume and the bid-ask spread in the first 15 minutes before sizing the satellite; most retail investors skip this step and end up paying the spread twice—once on entry and again on the quarterly rebalance. The biggest mistake with core-satellite is letting a satellite position grow past 25% of the total account without trimming. Imagine you bought a mix of XIU and a few individual TSX names in January and now want to know whether your actual weights still match your targets after the recent rotation out of healthcare. The S&P five hundred ended at seven thousand four hundred thirty-one while the TSX Composite reached thirty-four thousand nine hundred thirty-eight.

Sticky inflation readings at four point two percent CPI and six point five percent PPI kept both the Bank of Canada and the Fed on hold with limited easing priced in.

Index inclusion effects, long-cycle infrastructure spending, and first-mover moats in healthcare also shaped positioning across the five trading sessions.

Marvell Technology's addition to the S&P five hundred at the end of June triggered a seven percent plus premarket jump illustrating how passive funds must rebalance regardless of valuation.

The strategy works best when the added stock already has sector momentum and above-average trading volume.

It carries the risk that the move reverses once the rebalancing is complete.

To implement screen for stocks with upcoming index announcements using your broker's news feed or ETF holdings reports.

Then size the position smaller than a pure fundamental trade because the catalyst has a known expiration.

Historical data shows these inclusion pops have delivered the strongest alpha in the first three trading sessions after announcement.

Risk management requires a tight stop just below the pre-announcement close once the initial surge fades.

Air Canada and the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers reached a tentative agreement on a new contract this week according to BNN Bloomberg. The deal covers approximately nine thousand workers across the carrier's operations and addresses wages, scheduling, and pension contributions that had been in dispute since the prior round of bargaining.

Both sides confirmed the agreement ends the immediate threat of job action that had been scheduled for later this month. Union leadership stated the package includes improvements to job security language and training provisions that were not in the previous contract. Air Canada indicated the tentative terms will now move to a ratification vote expected within the next several weeks.

The resolution removes one near-term labor overhang that had weighed on the stock during the first half of June.

Retailers including Ikea are accelerating expansion of small-format stores as a response to shifting consumer patterns and rising real-estate expenses. The Swedish furniture giant opened or announced more than forty compact urban locations in the past eighteen months across North America and Europe, each averaging roughly one-third the size of a traditional big-box outlet.

Company executives cited faster inventory turns and lower operating costs per square foot as the primary drivers behind the shift. BNN Bloomberg reported that similar moves are underway at other chains seeking to maintain physical presence in high-density neighborhoods without the capital outlay of full-size stores.

Early results show these locations achieve higher sales per square foot while requiring fewer staff hours to operate. The trend coincides with post-pandemic changes in shopping behavior that favor quick in-and-out visits over large-format browsing.

Earnings reports scheduled for the coming week include Canopy Growth and Kroger, both of which will provide fresh data on consumer staples margins under the latest producer-price pressures. Canopy Growth is expected to release quarterly results that will show whether recent cost-cutting measures have offset continued softness in recreational cannabis demand.

Kroger will report on grocery pricing power and same-store sales trends after the six point five percent PPI print highlighted elevated input costs across the sector. Analysts will watch both companies for any commentary on how higher energy and packaging expenses are being passed through to customers without triggering volume declines.

The releases arrive ahead of the Bank of Canada’s July fifteenth decision and could influence sentiment toward defensive equity sleeves. Investors using TFSA accounts can monitor these names for potential margin-expansion signals that align with the inflation-protected strategy discussed earlier.

Another city has deployed additional transit police to address safety concerns and fare evasion, according to BNN Bloomberg reporting. The initiative follows similar programs in other major North American municipalities that have reported measurable reductions in incidents after increasing officer presence on platforms and trains.

City officials cited a twenty-three percent rise in fare-evasion complaints over the past year as the immediate trigger for the expanded deployment. The program includes both uniformed patrols and plain-clothes enforcement teams focused on high-traffic corridors.

Local transit authorities indicated the added staffing is funded through a combination of municipal budget reallocations and provincial grants. The move reflects broader municipal efforts to restore rider confidence after pandemic-era ridership declines.

Meta continues internal efforts to commercialize the new AI model developed after hiring Alexandr Wang a year ago, according to CNBC. Wang, previously founder of Scale AI, was brought in to accelerate Meta’s large-language-model capabilities, yet the company has struggled to integrate the resulting technology into its core advertising and consumer products.

Mark Zuckerberg has taken direct responsibility for driving adoption across business units, a shift that underscores the gap between model development and monetization. Internal documents obtained by CNBC show that early versions of the model achieved competitive benchmark scores but lacked clear use cases that justified additional infrastructure spend.

The episode illustrates the execution risk that remains even after high-profile talent acquisitions in the AI space. Canadian investors tracking global tech exposure may note the story as a reminder that hiring announcements alone do not guarantee near-term revenue contribution.

President Trump is traveling to the G7 summit in France with the Iran deal and Ukraine on the formal agenda, CNBC reported. The meetings occur against the backdrop of reported progress toward ending the Iran conflict that already produced a four percent drop in oil prices this week.

European leaders are expected to press for coordinated energy-security measures should the deal hold, while the Ukraine file remains a separate track with limited linkage to the current ceasefire talks. White House officials indicated the summit will also address tariff and trade issues that have resurfaced after the recent inflation prints.

Markets will watch for any language that signals follow-through commitments versus rhetorical progress. The outcome could influence whether the current oil-price relief proves durable into July.

On Sunday with markets closed we use this time to reflect on how the week's themes connect rather than update any single simulated position.

The Iran deal breakthrough and the inflation prints together show why energy exposure and pricing-power screens deserve ongoing attention heading into next week.

This is a simulated trade for learning purposes and we will watch for follow-through volume in index-added names and infrastructure suppliers on Monday.

One simulated position entered on Monday open and exited Friday close captured a portion of the rebound in financial names tied to IPO expectations.

When the first tranche shows a five percent gain and volume exceeds the twenty-day average that is the precise moment to consider adding rather than letting emotion drive size.

The XLF sector ETF on pullbacks to the fifty-day moving average remains the cleanest way for Canadian investors to access bank trading revenue inside TFSA limits.

Watch for follow-through volume in financials and infrastructure names plus any shift in Bank of Canada language at the July fifteenth decision.

The practical takeaway is to keep position sizes modest on catalyst-driven trades and to use volume confirmation before adding to any winner.

That wraps up today's Modern Investing Techniques. Remember, every trade is a learning opportunity, win or lose. Imagine you own 100 shares of Royal Bank of Canada trading at $145 and you want extra income while you hold through a quiet summer. You sell one covered call with a $150 strike expiring in 30 days and collect a $2.10 premium; your effective sale price becomes $152.10 if the stock is called away. That premium is compensation for giving someone else the right to buy your shares at $150. A call gives the buyer the right to purchase at the strike; a put gives the buyer the right to sell at the strike. The two Greeks that matter most for covered-call writers are delta (how much the option price moves with the stock) and theta (how much value the option loses each day as expiration approaches). > **SpaceX filed its S-1 on May 20 targeting a June 12 Nasdaq listing at roughly $1.8 trillion valuation; this episode gives retail investors a concrete plan across three time horizons.**
---
### Segment 1 — The Open
On May 20, 2026, Space Exploration Technologies Corp. filed its public S-1 registration statement with the SEC, converting months of draft-stage speculation into a concrete timeline that points to pricing around June 11 and first trading as early as June 12 under the ticker SPCX. By the end of this episode listeners will know exactly what the filing confirms about valuation targets, underwriters, and Starlink’s contribution to revenue, and they will leave with a practical three-horizon framework for deciding whether and how to participate once the stock begins trading.

### Segment 2 — The Background
SpaceX filed a confidential draft registration around April 1, 2026, then converted it to a public S-1 on May 20 under Registration No. 333-, making the prospectus available on EDGAR. Reporting from Reuters and CNBC indicates the company is aiming for a listing on Nasdaq as early as June 12, with the roadshow expected to begin around June 4 and pricing targeted for June 11. The valuation range discussed in recent coverage has settled around $1.75–2 trillion, with Bloomberg noting on May 29 that the target had been adjusted to “at least $1.8 trillion.” The deal is structured to include Starlink connectivity operations, launch and space services, and xAI, with Goldman Sachs serving as lead left bookrunner alongside Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Citigroup, and J.P. Morgan. Starlink generated $11.4 billion in revenue in 2025, representing 61 percent of the company’s $18.7 billion total and the only segment showing operating profit, while the overall business posted a net loss in Q1 2026. A potential retail allocation near 30 percent of the float has been mentioned in secondary commentary but remains unconfirmed in primary filings or major reporting. The 2026 IPO calendar features several large technology and AI-related offerings, creating a market backdrop of elevated investor interest in growth names even as interest-rate and risk sentiment remain mixed.

### Segment 3 — The Core Analysis
The S-1 shows that Elon Musk holds approximately 42 percent of equity but 85 percent of voting power, preserving control through a dual-class structure that will matter for governance questions after listing. Starlink is positioned as the cash-generative core, with more than 10 million subscribers and continued growth into Q1 2026, while launch operations and xAI continue to consume capital. Underwriters typically allocate the majority of shares to institutional clients in the initial offering, so most retail investors will obtain shares only after trading begins unless their broker offers a directed-share program. Reading the prospectus requires focus on revenue concentration, the path from operating income to free cash flow, use of proceeds, and any government-contract exposure that could affect margins. Canadian investors must also weigh TFSA, RRSP, or FHSA eligibility against the fact that the shares will trade in U.S. dollars, introducing currency risk that can be hedged or left unhedged depending on account type. Valuation discipline starts with comparing the targeted multiple to other high-growth technology names already public, recognizing that the $1.8 trillion figure implies aggressive assumptions about subscriber growth and launch economics. Platforms such as Interactive Brokers, Questrade, Wealthsimple, and Robinhood will likely offer post-listing access, but conditional offer-to-buy windows before pricing remain broker-specific and are not guaranteed. The filing does not yet detail exact retail allocation mechanics, so investors should monitor subsequent amendments and broker announcements rather than assume early access.

### Segment 4 — The Framework (How to Think About It / How to Act)
A disciplined short-term approach treats the opening days as the highest-risk window: first-day pops are common but frequently retrace, and wide bid-ask spreads plus potential volatility around the open make chasing the initial print expensive for anyone without a pre-set rule. Investors can decide in advance whether they will participate at all on day one or wait for volume to normalize, thereby removing emotion from the decision. In the medium term the 180-day lock-up expiry creates a predictable supply event when early investors and insiders become free to sell; waiting for that window or dollar-cost-averaging afterward has historically reduced entry prices for comparable names. The first two earnings reports as a public company will supply the initial evidence on whether Starlink margins and subscriber metrics translate cleanly into GAAP results. Over the long term the thesis rests on recurring satellite broadband revenue, Starship-driven launch cost reductions, and the broader total addressable market cited in the filing, balanced against key-person risk, ongoing capital intensity, and competition in both connectivity and launch markets. Canadians should consider whether a taxable account or a registered plan better accommodates the currency exposure and single-stock volatility limits they are willing to accept. Position sizing should reflect the difference between a diversified ETF holding and a concentrated growth name, with clear criteria for what subscriber or margin data would confirm or break the investment case over multiple years. The same horizon framework can be reused for any future large-cap IPO: define the entry rule for each period before the stock begins trading, then execute only according to those pre-written rules.

### Segment 5 — The Risks & The Other Side
Historical data on large IPOs shows that many names experience first-day gains followed by underperformance over the subsequent one to three years once lock-up supply arrives and fundamentals are tested in public reporting. The current research notes that some analysts view the valuation as aggressive relative to a sum-of-parts breakdown, while others highlight the optionality embedded in Starship economics and future businesses. Execution risk remains material because launch cadence, satellite deployment, and regulatory approvals for spectrum and orbital slots must continue at scale. Musk’s concentrated voting control reduces the ability of public shareholders to influence strategy, which can be viewed as either a strength or a governance concern depending on execution outcomes. Competition in satellite broadband from established and new entrants, plus the capital demands of both the launch and AI segments, could pressure margins even if Starlink grows. The base rate that IPOs tend to lag broad indices in the first few years after listing is well documented across multiple market cycles and should inform any position-size decision.

### Segment 6 — The Takeaways
Pre-define separate entry and sizing rules for the first trading week, the lock-up expiry window, and the multi-year hold period rather than reacting to price action. Focus first on the quality and concentration of revenue and the path to sustainable free cash flow in the S-1 before considering valuation multiples. Treat any single-name growth stock as a satellite position whose size is capped by personal volatility tolerance and overall portfolio construction rules. Watch for amendments to the S-1 and broker announcements on retail access in the coming weeks, then compare those details against the three-horizon framework before taking any action.

> **SpaceX has no announced IPO, yet the mechanics of how retail investors actually access or approach any future listing are worth mastering now.**
---
### Segment 1 — The Open
SpaceX continues to operate as a private company with a valuation shaped by tender offers rather than public markets, yet the question of how ordinary investors might one day participate remains relevant. This episode examines the current state of SpaceX exposure options alongside the broader, reusable process for evaluating any IPO. By the end, listeners will understand the realistic paths available today and carry a disciplined checklist for assessing newly public companies in either Canadian or U.S. accounts.

### Segment 2 — The Background
SpaceX was founded in 2002 and has grown into a major private aerospace firm whose Starlink satellite constellation now generates the majority of its revenue through broadband services, while the core launch business supplies launch capacity and government contracts. The company has raised successive rounds of private capital and conducted periodic tender offers that allow existing shareholders to sell shares to new investors at negotiated prices. These tenders have produced reported valuations in the range of $200 billion or higher in recent years, though exact figures fluctuate with each transaction and remain non-public. Elon Musk has repeatedly stated a preference for keeping the company private to avoid quarterly reporting pressures and short-term market demands. No formal IPO registration or pricing has been announced as of late May 2026, making any discussion of a public listing speculative. Retail investors therefore face two distinct questions: how to gain any exposure while the firm stays private, and how to approach an eventual public offering if one occurs. The second question applies far beyond SpaceX and forms the reusable framework that occupies the second half of this episode.

### Segment 3 — The Core Analysis
Traditional IPOs involve a company filing an S-1 registration statement with the SEC, selecting underwriters who market the shares through a roadshow, and ultimately pricing the offering after collecting indications of interest from institutional buyers. The first-day “pop” often occurs because the offering price is set conservatively to ensure the deal clears, leaving room for immediate trading gains once public supply and demand take over. Direct listings bypass the underwritten allocation process and allow existing shares to trade immediately on an exchange, while SPACs reverse-merge a private company into a publicly traded shell, each route carrying different costs, timelines, and allocation outcomes for retail participants. Retail investors rarely receive meaningful allocations at the IPO price because underwriters prioritize large institutions; most individuals must buy in the open market after trading begins, frequently at a premium to the initial offering price. Post-IPO lock-up agreements typically prevent insiders and early investors from selling for 180 days, after which a wave of supply can pressure the stock if those holders choose to exit. The S-1 itself contains the prospectus that details revenue recognition policies, customer concentration, capital structure, dilution from convertible securities or options, and the use of proceeds; disciplined readers focus on these sections rather than the summary marketing language. Historical studies of IPO cohorts show that, on average, newly public companies have underperformed broad market indices over the subsequent one-to-three years, with the effect most pronounced among firms that price at peak valuation multiples or operate in crowded sectors. Canadian investors face the additional layer of currency conversion and the choice between TFSA, RRSP, or taxable accounts, each carrying different tax treatment for foreign dividends and capital gains. Platforms that facilitate pre-IPO access, such as Forge Global or EquityZen, generally require accredited-investor status and impose minimum investments that place them out of reach for most retail participants. Funds or holding companies that carry SpaceX stakes exist but often trade at premiums or discounts to net asset value and may carry their own liquidity restrictions. Waiting for a public listing, if one materializes, therefore remains the most straightforward route for the majority of individual investors.

### Segment 4 — The Framework
A disciplined investor begins by confirming whether any IPO candidate meets basic criteria of revenue visibility, a credible path to sustained free cash flow, and a share structure that limits excessive dilution. Before committing capital, the same investor reviews the S-1 for related-party transactions, insider ownership percentages, and the size of the lock-up overhang relative to daily trading volume. Account selection follows: a TFSA or RRSP may suit longer-term Canadian holdings where contribution room exists, while a taxable account offers loss-harvesting flexibility if the position is held only briefly. Retail platforms such as Interactive Brokers, Questrade, or Wealthsimple allow post-IPO purchases in either CAD or USD, yet none provide allocation at the offering price. The investor then asks whether the current valuation already prices in optimistic growth assumptions and whether comparable public companies trade at materially lower multiples. Common mistakes include chasing the first-day pop without reviewing lock-up expiration dates, ignoring currency risk on U.S.-listed names, or treating an IPO as inherently different from any other equity purchase. The framework generalizes: apply the same revenue-quality and dilution screens to every newly public company, regardless of sector or headline appeal, and consider a waiting period of several quarters to observe post-lock-up trading behavior and earnings delivery. This approach treats IPOs as one subset of equity opportunities rather than a distinct asset class requiring special rules.

### Segment 5 — The Risks & The Other Side
The strongest bull case for any high-profile listing rests on the possibility that early revenue traction and technological leadership translate into durable market share, yet historical base rates show many such companies later face margin compression or competitive response once public scrutiny increases. The bear case highlights the documented tendency of IPOs to underperform in the years after listing, driven by both initial over-optimism and the eventual release of locked-up shares. Private-market platforms carry their own frictions: accreditation requirements, high minimums, wide bid-ask spreads, and the risk that the platform itself faces liquidity or regulatory issues. Even if SpaceX eventually lists, the timing, pricing, and lock-up terms remain unknown, so any current exposure through indirect vehicles carries basis risk relative to a future public share price. Currency movements between CAD and USD add another layer of volatility for Canadian investors holding U.S. securities. None of these considerations constitute a prediction; they simply illustrate that the range of outcomes is wide and that past cohort performance offers only probabilistic guidance rather than certainty.

### Segment 6 — The Takeaways
Rule one: treat any unannounced IPO as speculative and evaluate exposure routes on their actual accessibility and cost rather than anticipated future liquidity. Rule two: read the S-1 for revenue concentration, dilution mechanics, and lock-up size before considering any post-IPO purchase. Rule three: default to waiting several quarters after listing to observe trading behavior once insiders can sell. Rule four: apply the same account-type and position-sizing discipline used for any equity, recognizing that IPOs carry no special exemption from ordinary market risk. Watch for the next concrete filing of an S-1 by a company with meaningful private-market visibility; that document will provide the first verifiable data set on which to test the framework.
